label: Displacement Convexity in the Curved Case
notes: Chapter 16 made the entropy convex along Wasserstein geodesics in flat space; this chapter carries that picture onto a curved manifold. The bookkeeping changes because volumes distort along geodesics. We introduce dimension-sensitive convexity classes and distortion coefficients so the entropy story survives positive and negative Ricci curvature alike.

label: From Flat to Curved
notes: On Euclidean space McCann interpolation moves mass along straight lines and volumes are preserved, so convexity of the entropy reduces to a one-dimensional fact. On a manifold the same interpolation rides geodesics, and a thin bundle of geodesics spreads or focuses depending on curvature. That focusing is precisely what the distortion coefficients must record.

label: Distortion Coefficients
notes: The distortion coefficient compares the actual Jacobian of the geodesic interpolation to the model space of constant curvature K and dimension N. When the bundle of geodesics spreads more than the flat baseline the coefficient exceeds one; when curvature focuses it, the coefficient drops below one. These coefficients are the curved replacement for the trivial flat factor.

label: The Reference Measure
notes: Entropy is never absolute; it is measured against a fixed reference measure, here the Riemannian volume. The density of a transported measure with respect to that volume is what enters the entropy functional. Changing the reference measure changes the effective curvature seen by the entropy, which is the seed of weighted manifolds and the Bakry-Emery tensor.

label: Displacement Convexity Classes DC_N
notes: A nonlinearity U lies in the class DC_N when its pressure-rescaled form is convex in the appropriate variable. This single algebraic condition is exactly what lets U interact correctly with the distortion coefficients of dimension N. Boltzmann entropy and the Renyi-type functionals are the canonical members that drive the geometric inequalities.

label: Ricci Lower Bound Meets Dimension Upper Bound
notes: Two inputs combine: a Ricci curvature bounded below by K times the metric, and a manifold dimension at most N. The lower curvature bound controls how much geodesics may focus, while the dimension cap limits how many independent directions can focus at once. Together they pin down the model distortion coefficients beta from below.

label: The Distortion Coefficients beta_t^{K,N}
notes: For positive K the coefficient uses a sine profile whose argument scales with the geodesic length and the square root of K over N minus one. For negative K it uses the hyperbolic sine. At K equal to zero it collapses to the flat factor t. These closed forms are the model-space yardstick the inequality measures against.

label: The Convexity Inequality
notes: The central estimate bounds the entropy at the midpoint, and more generally along the geodesic, by a beta-weighted combination of the endpoint entropies. The distortion coefficients enter inside the convexity, replacing the naive linear interpolation. This is the precise curved analogue of the flat displacement convexity inequality from the previous chapter.

label: K-Convexity of the Entropy
notes: When the distortion correction is absorbed, the entropy is K-convex along every Wasserstein geodesic: its second difference is bounded below by K times the squared transport distance. A positive K makes the entropy uniformly convex, which forces contraction of the heat flow and underlies functional inequalities like log-Sobolev and Talagrand.

label: The Curvature-Dimension Condition CD(K,N)
notes: Lott, Villani, and Sturm turn the inequality into a definition: a metric measure space satisfies CD(K,N) when the entropy is displacement convex with the beta coefficients for those parameters. On a smooth manifold this is equivalent to the Ricci and dimension bounds, but it requires no smoothness, so it transports curvature to singular spaces.

label: Computational Footprint
notes: The notebook makes the abstract condition inspectable. It plots distortion curves for several K and N choices, with the flat coefficient as a baseline, and checks numerically that positive curvature stays below that baseline before conjugate effects appear. A finite transport plan with conserved mass anchors the geometry to verifiable bookkeeping.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We assembled the curved displacement-convexity machine: distortion coefficients, the DC_N classes, the beta-weighted inequality, and the synthetic CD(K,N) condition. The reference measure choice ties it to weighted geometry. Next chapters exploit K-convexity to derive sharp Sobolev, Talagrand, and concentration inequalities, and to stabilize curvature under measured Gromov-Hausdorff limits.
